title: Retirement spending constrained despite guaranteed pension income
full_text:
Uncertainty about future health and aged care costs is prompting State Super members to limit retirement spending, even as defined benefit pensions provide confidence about their regular income.
The fund’s Member Perspectives 2026 white paper found rising living expenses and financial support for family members were also shaping retirement budgets, with some members reconsidering their plans or delaying retirement.
The findings drew on three member advisory forums conducted from late 2024 into 2026, involving 225 working and retired members across NSW public sector agencies, including education, health, police, emergency services and transport.
Members consistently valued the certainty of a defined benefit pension, including its protection against the risk of outliving their income and the security provided by annual inflation indexation.
However, that confidence failed to alleviate concerns about unexpected medical bills, private health insurance premiums or the potential cost of entering aged care.
“You can’t predict a medical emergency where you have to go private, as you can’t wait for public hospital treatment, and end up out of pocket thousands of dollars,” one member said.
The report found many members were saving to prepare for uncertain medical expenses, recognising they would spend more and enjoy retirement more if those concerns did not exist.
Another member described the difficulty of estimating the savings required: “You just don’t know how much you need as the buffer against unforeseen future expenses”.
Concerns about aged care included the lump sum required to enter a facility and whether sufficient savings would remain later in life.
“I think by the time you’re in your 90s, I think most of us probably would not have a large amount left in our retirement funds. So, I think that’s a stress for the future because how long’s a piece of string? I think that’s something that as we do age better, I think is in the back of many of our minds,” one member said.
Rising everyday expenses were also affecting members despite annual pension indexation, particularly insurance and electricity costs.
One member was considering reducing private health insurance despite having a chronic health condition, while another had delayed retirement to fund home improvements, including solar panels, intended to reduce future expenses.
Alongside their own needs, members described supporting adult children, grandchildren and elderly parents through housing deposits, groceries, education, bills and caring responsibilities.
Some said that assistance had exceeded their expectations and required them to reconsider retirement finances, while others questioned whether they could afford to help children enter the housing market.
State Super chief executive John Livanas said the findings would inform the fund’s planning and contribute to broader industry efforts to support Australians preparing for retirement.
“This research provides valuable insights into how retirees think about financial wellbeing and the challenges they face. We hope these findings contribute to the broader industry conversation and help shape a retirement system that is more responsive to the needs and expectations of future retirees.
“In our forums, members reflected deeply on the confidence and peace of mind a defined benefit pension provides and the certainty of a regular income when planning for retirement.”
The forums also highlighted the importance of purpose, social connections and suitable housing, with older retirees encouraging younger members to set aside money to enjoy retirement while their health allowed.
State Super had more than 76,000 members and $37 billion in assets at 30 June 2026, with around 82 per cent of members receiving a defined benefit pension.
